Competitive Authoritarianism In America
articles.abstract: Abstract: The United States crossed the line into competitive authoritarianism during Donald Trump's second presidency: Elections remained real, but incumbents systematically abused state institutions to tilt the playing field against opponents. The administration weaponized the Justice Department, the FBI, and other agencies against critics, universities, law firms, and the press, while national gerrymandering and coerced corporate money skewed competition. Judged by the eleven criteria the authors devised to score 35 regimes in their earlier research, the U.S. case is comparable to Hungary under Viktor Orbán, if far softer than 1990s Russia or Serbia. The new regime is unlikely to consolidate, however: The United States’ vast countervailing power—its wealth, private sector, and civil society—dilutes authoritarian abuse and makes redemocratization by electoral turnover likely. Yet turnover would not mean democracy survived intact. Opposition parties do win unfair elections, and a restored U.S. democracy will remain unconsolidated until both major parties commit to its defense.

articles.title: Does Nonviolent Action Still Work?
articles.abstract: Abstract: From Burma to Belarus, one question keeps surfacing: Does nonviolent action still work? The authors argue that the theory hasn’t failed, but rather that the field has fallen behind. Authoritarian regimes have modernized repression while movements have reduced strategic nonviolent struggle to street protest, mistaking visibility for leverage. That gap helps explain why organizers facing lethal repression have turned to arms, even though nonviolent campaigns still outperform violent ones. The authors also challenge how success gets measured: Leader-centric, single-cycle standards obscure real gains. What the field needs now isn’t new doctrine but investment in countering smart repression, rebuilding noncooperation, and sharing lessons across movements.

articles.title: The Real Liberation Technology
articles.abstract: Abstract: Larry Diamond’s “liberation technology”—the internet and social media—has not freed closed regimes: Autocrats own the off switch and weaponize it. The real liberation technology is the democratization of finance. Unlike social media, digital payments are incentive-compatible: They enlarge the economy autocrats live off, so rulers promote them even while blocking the internet. Yet they erode authoritarian rents and create a new digital bourgeoisie whose demand for the rule of law—when it is a challenger, not an incumbent—drives political change. Grounded in evidence from Findex, mobile money, and tax revolts, the argument reframes how outsiders can support democratic evolution.

articles.title: Authoritarian AI’s Last-Mile Problem
articles.abstract: Abstract: Is artificial intelligence the autocrats’ silver bullet? No. AI-empowered autocrats are constrained by the “last-mile problem”: AI can help regimes to see, sort, and predict, but human police officers, soldiers, and local officials remain indispensable for physical coercion. In the long run, human agents will stay relevant: They not only guarantee an effective repressive system but also signal the autocrats’ popularity. For prodemocracy actors, this suggests that the conventional wisdom on combating autocracies, such as encouraging defections among security forces, still holds. The bottom line: Repression in the AI era remains a human affair.

articles.title: Will AI Surveillance End Bureaucratic Autonomy?
articles.abstract: Abstract: Civil servants are a neglected source of democratic resilience. Their partial autonomy lets them resist abuses of state power. This resistance is possible because politicians cannot perfectly observe bureaucrats’ preferences or behavior. Artificial intelligence is closing this gap. States are collecting more data on their own officials, and AI tools can merge and analyze extensive records that once sat in separate systems. Illiberal leaders can now identify and punish bureaucrats they consider disloyal at scale. Drawing on cases from democracies and authoritarian regimes, this article argues that the legal architecture protecting bureaucratic autonomy must be updated for the data age.

articles.title: The Age of Authoritarian Abundance
articles.authors: Senem Aydın-Düzgit, Berk Esen, Sebnem Gumuscu
articles.abstract: Abstract: This essay argues that the post-unipolar international order, combined with unprecedented interdependence, has created an “age of authoritarian abundance.” As the relative power of the United States and Europe declines and democratic erosion spreads within the West, Western governments increasingly repurpose their influence toward transactional partnerships with illiberal actors. At the same time, autocrats can draw political, financial, technological, and diplomatic support from a diverse array of great powers, authoritarian middle powers, international institutions, and private firms, reducing dependence on any single patron and exploiting asymmetries in areas such as migration, energy, and digital infrastructure. These mutually reinforcing trends expand the resources available for autocratic survival while leaving prodemocracy forces with little external support. Democracy’s prospects are not foreclosed, but in a fragmented order without a major power committed to promoting democratic norms, they depend on many actors whose interests rarely align with democratic ends.

articles.title: Why Welfare States Save Democracy
articles.abstract: Abstract: Rising inequality threatens democratic durability, as societies become increasingly polarized. South Korea and Taiwan have resisted global trends in democratic backsliding by continually expanding their social welfare regimes. Democratic resilience and welfare deepening have been mutually reinforcing in South Korea and Taiwan. Democratization during the 1990s created the political conditions and incentives to deepen the government’s social policy commitments. Over the past three decades, the continued expansion of the social safety nets in South Korea and Taiwan has mitigated the effects of growing inequality and deepened citizens’ trust in democratic institutions and practices.

articles.title: Polarization Is Not the Problem
articles.abstract: Abstract: Partisan polarization is not the greatest threat to U.S. democracy, but a symptom of a deeper struggle over who belongs and deserves equal rights. Rapid gains by racial minorities, women, and LGBTQ citizens have produced an ethnonationalist backlash whose adherents now wield disproportionate power through the Republican Party. This conflict has intensified partisan animosity and moral disengagement, but a “both sides” diagnosis obscures the asymmetry between a faction seeking to reverse social progress and those resisting it. Polarization is therefore less the disease than democracy’s immune response to an unpopular, antidemocratic movement. Suppressing that response in the name of civility would only strengthen the movement and imperil pluralistic self-government. The United States can still become its most inclusive democracy, but only if leaders defend equal rights and voters hold accountable those who will not.

articles.title: Taiwan’s Deadlocked Democracy
articles.abstract: Abstract: In May 2024, Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te took office while facing off against an opposition party majority in the legislature. Since then, the island has been caught in a slowly escalating constitutional crisis. The Constitutional Court is now paralyzed, key regulatory bodies sit vacant, the annual budget bill is a half-year late, and the premier has refused to countersign legislation. This political dysfunction has been blamed on nationalist polarization, PRC influence, or reckless and irresponsible opposition parties, but these explanations overlook a simpler cause: Taiwan’s institutions are simply not well-designed to handle divided government. The political system lacks adequate safeguards to protect the independence of accountability institutions. Unified government masked this design flaw for many years, but it now threatens Taiwan’s democracy.

articles.title: Democratic Resistance in Eroding Democracies
How to Build the Right Coalition
articles.abstract: Abstract: In competitive authoritarian and autocratic contexts, political parties win elections more frequently by running as public unity coalitions. However, in eroding democracies, voters are often highly polarized. The incumbent often won because the main opposition party was disliked by a plurality or majority of voters. Joining with such a tainted party can harm candidates’ chances. Where elected leaders are eroding once-strong democracies, opposition parties often do better with quiet coalitions in which parties remain fully independent but work together; choosing not to run against one another, or competing electorally to offer voters’ choice, but promising to caucus together post-election.

articles.title: How to Protect the Media in Eroding Democracies
articles.abstract: Abstract: Independent media is not merely one institution among those under attack in eroding democracies; it is the connective tissue linking the electoral, institutional, and popular forms of resistance on which democratic survival depends. Yet the terrain has shifted: A media ecosystem once defined by scarcity and dispersed ownership is now fractured, networked, and funneled through a few platforms that capture most digital-advertising revenue. Comparing democratic decline in Hungary, India, Poland, and Sri Lanka, the author finds that erosion ran deepest where governments dominated digital-media ecosystems—India's ruling party built a propaganda “machine” on WhatsApp, while Hungary's never achieved comparable dominance online, leaving room for Péter Magyar's challenge. Five lessons follow: win the battle for digital distribution, build networked media ecosystems before they are needed, diversify media-financing models, develop legal-defense infrastructures, and connect institutional erosion to citizens' everyday concerns. The question is no longer whether journalism survives, but whether independent media can still help citizens discover common interests and act on them.

articles.title: How Courts Survive Democratic Backsliding
articles.abstract: Abstract: When elected leaders attack the courts, why does judicial independence sometimes survive? This essay argues that courts rarely prevent executive power grabs on their own. Rather, judges depend on judicial allies—especially legislators, civil society groups, and international actors—who empower courts to resist executive aggrandizement. By analyzing cross-national evidence as well as case studies of Brazil, Israel, and Poland, the author finds that judicial independence is most resilient when opposition parties retain power in the legislature. Yet even when illiberal governments control the legislature, protests and international actors can still protect the courts. The case studies illustrate that mobilization by judicial allies often generates positive feedback effects, as mobilization empowers judges, whose decisions energize further resistance. At a time when courts are under attack in the United States and globally, judicial allies must not only defend courts but also, in the longer term, reform them.

articles.title: How to Break an Autocrat’s Coalition
articles.abstract: Abstract: Authoritarian coalitions look unbreakable, but they are not: Allies defect when the costs of loyalty rise and the costs of defection fall, and opposition parties and civil society can engineer both. Moderate institutional strategies—contesting elections, courts, and legislatures—force stealth autocrats to abandon their democratic façade, as in Guatemala, where Bernardo Arévalo's Semilla party stayed on the 2023 ballot and pushed the elite alliance known as the “Corrupt Pact” into overt manipulation that split it. Persistent journalism makes loyalty reputationally costly, as years of corruption reporting in Hungary did before Péter Magyar broke with Viktor Orbán. Depolarization lowers the price of defecting, as when Colombia's opposition refused Alvaro Uribe's provocations, or when Indiana activists sent thank-you notes to Republicans resisting mid-decade redistricting. Such wins are partial—Uribe's chosen successor still won—but defections that build “broad thin coalitions” across ideological lines do shift power, and marginal gains are worth the effort.

articles.title: How Protest Can Halt Backsliding
articles.abstract: Abstract: Mass protest can halt democratic backsliding, but only when it shifts political power away from autocratizing incumbents before they become entrenched. Comparing Brazil, Georgia, Poland, Serbia, and South Korea, this essay identifies three pathways through which protest can make that shift: Empowering institutional actors to curb executive overreach, mobilizing previously disengaged citizens to vote, and eroding support for incumbents among voters and elites. Success depends less on the sheer size of demonstrations than on whether organizers reach beyond the existing opposition, counter polarizing government narratives, and connect street mobilization to effective parties, legislators, and electoral strategies. Where opposition parties are weak, institutions captured, and repression advanced, even sustained mass mobilization may not yield an immediate breakthrough. Protest should therefore be treated as one tool in a broader democracy-defense strategy—one that can slow authoritarian consolidation, build civic capacity, and prepare future electoral or institutional openings.

articles.title: Survival Before Diplomacy: How Electoral Competition Constrains Leader Diplomacy in Turkey
articles.abstract: Do election campaigns reduce leaders’ engagement in foreign diplomacy? Whereas existing research argues that elections divert leaders’ time and attention away from international affairs, most evidence comes from the United States and relies on yearly data. This article examines the relationship between electoral cycles and diplomatic travel using the case of Turkey. Drawing on a monthly dataset of official foreign visits by Turkish prime ministers, presidents, and foreign ministers between 1990 and 2025, the analysis reveals that foreign travel declines significantly during election months and the immediately preceding period. The effect is strongest for top leaders, although foreign ministers also reduce travel. By using high-frequency data from a non-US case, the article provides new evidence on how domestic electoral pressures shape foreign-policy activity.

articles.title: Gender-Role Traditionalism and Opposition to Trade in the United States
articles.abstract: A recently popular line in American trade politics is that free trade threatens male blue-collar manufacturing employment, thereby undermining “traditional” family gender roles in which men work outside of the home and women work as caregivers within it. This study asks whether American mass politics mirrors these ideas. Does a preference for “traditional” gender roles lead Americans to protectionism? Our analysis of American National Election Studies data suggests that it does. We find a significant and highly robust empirical relationship between gender conservatism and protectionism. That relationship has been evident since 2008 and it decidedly is not a product of Trump-era politics. That relationship holds among men and women and among Republicans and Democrats, and it is robust to the inclusion of controls meant to isolate gender conservatism from other expressions of conservatism. The recent rise of gender-conservative trade skepticism should be understood as elite politics catching up with the public rather than leading it.

Candidate Gender and District Ideological Alignment in U.S. Congressional Elections, 2002–2020
articles.abstract: Candidate ideology impacts a wide range of electoral outcomes, but are there gendered differences in the effects of candidate ideology? Using a unique dataset of U.S. congressional elections between 2002 and 2020, we examine candidate-level factors (gender, ideology, and partisanship) and district-level political factors (district ideology and partisanship), and the interaction between these candidate and district-level factors. We first compare two measurements of candidate ideology for congressional incumbents of both major parties: absolute extremity and ideological distance from the district. Although there are partisan differences, we generally find that women are more ideologically extreme than men. We then examine how ideological distance from the district impacts three dependent variables, likelihood of running unopposed, vote share, and probability of winning election, and test how candidate gender interacts with ideological distance from the district. We find that incumbent women are less likely to run unopposed and have a lower vote share than incumbent men. Overall, it appears that women congressional candidates may be more ideologically extreme and are more likely to be punished for their ideological positions than men.

articles.title: Leveraging National Party Leaders in Congressional Campaigns: The Case of Nancy Pelosi
articles.authors: Nichole M. Bauer, Erin C. Cassese, Natalie M. Standridge
articles.abstract: Existing scholarship on negative campaigning has focused on the communication strategies of candidates who are actively contesting specific seats or offices. Yet, political leaders are often featured in ads where they are not a contestant. For example, between 2018 and 2022, the Republican Party spent over 227 million dollars on negative campaign ads featuring Nancy Pelosi, hoping to capitalize on her unpopularity with a wide swath of the voting public. In this paper, we develop a theoretical perspective on this kind of attack by association that emphasizes two processes – ideological signposting and transfer of affect – to explain why campaigns might choose to adopt this strategy. Using Pelosi as a case study, we analyze her depictions in televised U.S. House race ads from 2010 to 2020 and compare them with similarly situated male Congressional leaders. Our approach blends a content analysis of the visual and verbal elements of campaign ads with metadata from the Wesleyan Media Project, providing insights into the conditions under which attacks against Pelosi are likely to emerge. Our findings have implications for understanding not only negative campaigning but also the nationalization of political discourse and the challenges facing women as they advance to leadership positions within Congress.

articles.title: How members and elites make sense of ideological change: Natural evolution, pragmatic adaptation, or betrayal in the (Northern) League
articles.abstract: How do party members and representatives make sense of ideological change? This article tackles this question by studying one of the most important party transformations in contemporary European politics: the shift of the (Northern) League from populist regionalism to populist radical right politics under Matteo Salvini. Drawing on 60 semi-structured in-depth interviews with members and representatives, the analysis identifies three recurrent narratives: natural evolution (the national turn as the completion of the federalist project), pragmatic adaptation (change as electorally and strategically necessary), and betrayal (a rupture with the founding identity). The survival of the residual Padanian identity is no longer sustained by ideology, but loosely surfaces in rituals such as the annual gathering at Pontida, where it is blended with the state-wide symbolism. The findings suggest that the mass party model has facilitated the transformation while preventing overt infighting. This invites further research into the interpretive work during party change.

articles.title: Different articles, similar arguments: A response to Rosenberg
articles.abstract: In this short response to Rosenberg (2026), we focus on three points. First, we note that there is now agreement that intra-party sortition is unlikely to deliver a more socially representative legislature without some other measures such as stratification or quotas. Second, we argue that it is curious to criticise us for not considering the possibility of change in the future in response to the introduction of intra-party sortition, when we did exactly that at some length in our original article. And third, we raise a broader issue about exactly how scholars might measure the overall representativeness of an institution.

The Global Carbon Budget as a cointegrated system
articles.authors: Mikkel Bennedsen, Eric Hillebrand, Morten Ørregaard Nielsen
articles.abstract: Summary The Global Carbon Budget, maintained by the Global Carbon Project, summarizes Earth’s global carbon cycle through four annual time series beginning in 1959: atmospheric CO2 concentrations, anthropogenic CO2 emissions, and CO2 uptake by land and by ocean. We analyze these four time series as a multivariate (cointegrated) system. Statistical tests show that the four time series are cointegrated with rank three and identify anthropogenic CO2 emissions as the single stochastic trend driving the non-stationary dynamics of the system. The three cointegrated relations correspond to the physical relations that the sinks are linearly related to atmospheric concentrations and that the change in concentrations equals emissions minus the combined uptake by land and ocean. Furthermore, likelihood ratio tests show that a parametrically restricted error-correction model that embodies these physical relations cannot be rejected on the data. The model can be used for both in-sample and out-of-sample analysis. In an application of the latter, we demonstrate that projections based on this model, using Shared Socioeconomic Pathways scenarios, yield results consistent with established climate science.

articles.title: ‘Change at home and change abroad?’ Visualising the (im)possibilities of British foreign policy in the aftermath of Corbyn’s response to the Manchester Arena bombing
articles.abstract: The Manchester Arena bombing occurred at a moment of heightened anxiety and uncertainty in the United Kingdom. One of several attacks over a matter of months in 2017, it was the deadliest and most politically affronting. The bombing brought the consequences of liberal interventionism into focus and triggered a contest to define the moment, producing competing visions of Britishness. Drawing on insights from Lacanian international relations and visual politics, the article analyses responses to the bombing through a multimodal discourse analysis of national newspaper coverage and political speeches. It shows that Jeremy Corbyn challenged the elite liberal-interventionist consensus by linking foreign intervention to terrorism at home and advocating policies of restraint, sovereign equality and democratic multilateralism. Resonating with sections of the public, Corbyn’s response generated acute anxiety among elites and elicited an affectively charged defence of the status quo. In response, politicians and legacy media sought to construct ideological equivalences between Corbyn and hostile Others, mobilising multimodal presentations which recast him as anti-British and a threat to national security. This article contributes to debates on continuity and change in British foreign policy and the role of images in managing dissent.

articles.title: The culture of political connections, financing constraints, and performance: firm-level evidence from Pakistan
articles.authors: Saira Qasim, Marian Rizov, Xufei Zhang
articles.abstract: This article examines how firm political connections affect the financing constraints of Pakistani firms, and how these are related to firm performance. Using panel data for the listed, non-financial, Pakistani firms, over the 2007–15 period, our empirical analysis shows that in Pakistan formal political connections affect significantly firm financial status: politically connected firms are less financially constrained. The results are consistent across various measures of financial status. We find, however, evidence that politically connected firms perform worse than unconnected firms. The results are robust to three different measures of firm performance. We also find some evidence that the effects of political connections on firm performance vary across groups of Pakistani firms by the level of financing constraint. Our results suggest financial resource misallocation in Pakistan consistent with the soft-budget constraint theory.

articles.title: The curious genealogy of stranded assets: how deregulation debates invented ‘stranding’
articles.abstract: Over the last 15 years, the concept of stranded assets has become increasingly prominent in analysis of the climate crisis and green transition. This study examines the history of this concept, drawing on databases of digitized publications to show how the language of ‘stranding’ was first systematically applied to asset-related losses in the 1980s. It documents how this terminology originated in US debates around public utility deregulation, where a diagnosis of ‘stranding’ helped to justify compensation in situations where policy change imposed investment losses on private asset owners—foreshadowing similar claims in parts of contemporary climate discourse, despite such compensation threatening to turn the ‘polluter pays’ principle on its head. Yet, exploring the history of stranded assets also reveals how this reallocation of risk was contested, highlighting flaws in the case for compensating owners of fossil fuel-related assets today.

articles.title: The financialization of dowry: marriage, debt, and value in urban India
articles.abstract: The marriage practice of dowry has spread to all communities across India and is widely decried for its association with violence against women. Scholars have converged on the roles of stratification and status-seeking as explanations for its spread. Drawing on eighty-nine interviews and a 101-household survey in a southern Indian city, I show how dowry among urban poor minorities is being facilitated by a wide availability of informal loans, thanks to an elective affinity with financialization. It has also become a site of predatory extraction. I argue that as parents are compelled to quantify their daughters’ worth and pay higher cash values, dowry has the paradoxical effect of devaluing daughters rather than securing their status. This analysis helps refine theories of social status and everyday financialization by looking at gender and social reproduction in the Global South. Instead of homogenizing cultures, financialization merges with cultural traditions, creating new forms of inequality.

articles.title: Difference-in-Differences Estimation: A Quasi-Experimental Approach to Sustainable Development Interventions
articles.abstract: How can we rigorously assess whether sustainable development interventions affect conflict? This methodological note demonstrates the difference-in-differences (DID) approach as a powerful tool for strengthening causal inference regarding sustainable development projects and their broader social and political consequences. While DID has been widely used to study climate-related shocks, practical guidance for applying these methods to intentional development interventions remains limited. This research note explains the core logic of DID methods in accessible terms, outlines the statistical framework, and demonstrates the approach using hydropower development as an illustrative case. The analysis reveals how DID can capture localized effects of development interventions with stronger causal evidence than correlational methods by comparing subnational variation across countries. The findings highlight both the promise and the limitations of this methodology for scholars and practitioners working at the intersection of development and environmental politics.

articles.title: Evidence, Progress, and Research Gaps: The Link Between Climate Change, Security, and Conflicts
Introducing Audience Analysis into Just Securitization Theory: A Study of Climate Security Perceptions in Türkiye
articles.abstract: This article examines how the public and members of parliament in Türkiye perceive climate change as a security issue and asks whether their perceptions create favorable conditions for its just securitization. Drawing on a survey of 3,827 participants and semistructured interviews with twenty parliamentarians, the study integrates audience analysis into Rita Floyd’s just securitization theory (JST) by evaluating how audience perceptions align with its normative criteria. Theoretically, it bridges the ontological divide in securitization scholarship by combining the Copenhagen School’s constructivist account of threat construction with Floyd’s moral criteria. Findings show broad consensus across both audiences: climate skepticism is minimal, water and food security and extreme climate events are the prioritized implications, and human beings and ecosystems are the primary referent objects. Both audiences support stronger state action. The article argues that integrating audience perceptions into JST strengthens the societal legitimacy and practical viability of climate securitization.

articles.title: Here Come the Cartographers: Mapping the Seabed in the Digital Age
articles.authors: Elizabeth Havice, Lisa M. Campbell, Noella Gray
articles.abstract: Members of the international oceans science and governance community are working to accelerate the effort to finish a complete mapping of the seabed by 2030. Based on our observations at the One Ocean Science Congress and the Third United Nations Oceans Congress, in this piece, we review the knowledge, technological, and regulatory-based arguments made in support of this effort and contextualize these within the broader history of mapping that highlights the relationship between science-driven legibility of space and political-economic change. Overall, we find that proponents of mapping generally present the act as a depoliticized, technical exercise that offers a general “good” to society. We point to the ways that this approach obscures the politics of mapping and urge attention to the more-than-technical nature of mapping. The processes and outcomes of mapping cannot be assumed, and proponents of seabed mapping should account for the scrambled relations and contestations that mapping drives and reflects.

articles.title: On the Economization of Environmental Policy: Examining the Workings of Green Competitiveness in the Pursuit of Emissions Reduction
articles.abstract: Hybrid, transnational governance frameworks such as the European Union’s Renewable Energy Directive (EU-RED) are designed to shape production and trade practices in third countries by linking market access to compliance with sustainability criteria. Evidence on their effectiveness in these contexts, however, remains limited. This article examines why such frameworks often fail to achieve their environmental goals, focusing on EU-RED’s regulation of biofuels in the Argentina–EU biodiesel global value chain. We argue that EU-RED is based on a form of economization of environmental regulation that we define as “green competitiveness,” in which environmental performance becomes constitutive of competitive advantage rather than merely an external constraint. Economic actors in Argentina adopt this logic to strengthen their market positions, yet their strategies frequently decouple from meaningful environmental outcomes. By conceptually identifying the defining elements of green competitiveness and empirically analyzing their implementation in the case study, we show how these tensions manifest in concrete practices on the ground.

articles.title: Saving a Rainforest and Losing the World: Conservation and Displacement in the Global Tropics by Gregory M. Thaler
Existential Politics: Why Global Climate Institutions Are Failing and How to Fix Them by Jessica F. Green
Positional Blurring in Context: How Dimensionality and Ideology Constrain Strategy
articles.authors: Nicolás de la Cerda, Jacob R. Gunderson
articles.abstract: Positional blurring is a common and effective party strategy. It enables parties to downplay some issues while highlighting and clarifying their profile on others. However, we know little about how parties use this strategy outside European party systems, in which (right-wing) populist parties are particularly noteworthy for their blurred economic positions and clear cultural positions. Is that strategy inherent to populism or a reflection of context-specific incentives? This article uses data from Europe and Latin America to argue that populists tailor their strategies to the dimensionality of their party system and populism’s host ideology. We find that multidimensional party systems and exclusionary thick ideologies drive populists to blur their economic positions. Extending this research field beyond Europe for the first time, these findings show that populists are heterogeneous actors whose varied thick ideologies embedded in diverse political systems systematically constrain their strategic behavior.

articles.title: The Democracy–Decarbonization Dilemma: Can Climate Assemblies Provide an Escape Route?
articles.abstract: Meeting the goals of the Paris Agreement on climate change demands rapid and systemic economic transformation. Yet, contemporary democracies seem tragically ill-suited to this task. Proposals to insulate climate policy making from democratic control—for instance, through delegation to expert bodies—seem likely to fuel the rise of authoritarian populists, which is already eroding democratic norms and institutions. Deepening democratic engagement with the process of decarbonization may provide an escape route from this apparent “democracy–decarbonization dilemma.” In this vein, there has recently been much enthusiasm for climate assemblies. Such processes can have profound effects on their participants. But can they influence attitudes to democracy and support for ambitious climate policy among the wider public? We conduct a narrative review of the theoretical and empirical literature on democratic mini-publics (DMPs) to answer this question and critically reflect on our findings. We find that DMPs can influence the wider public’s attitudes toward democratic institutions and public policy to some extent. Yet, DMPs alone—even if well publicized—seem unlikely to be sufficient to stimulate the widespread shifts in knowledge, capacities, attitudes and behavior necessary to escape the democracy–decarbonization dilemma. We propose expanding the use, institutionalization, and orientation of DMPs—so that they become a widely recognized and routinized feature of deliberative systems, interacting with both governments and the wider citizenry—while advancing complementary democratic reform initiatives.

articles.title: Inattention, Information Provision, and (Failures of) Revealed Preference,
articles.abstract: Economists often estimate preferences by looking at how demand for an option changes as its attributes change or as beliefs about them change in response to information. I show in a multi-attribute induced-preference experiment that this method can be substantially biased due to differential inattention. Attention is systematically distorted at baseline, with participants reacting much more to some attributes than others. Further, attention is highly malleable: information telling participants about the value of a desirable attribute—even when the information is already known, transparently redundant, and explicitly randomly assigned—greatly increases attention to the attribute it describes and distracts from other attributes. It also boosts average demand for the good, implying that inattention takes the form of neglect rather than shrinkage toward a prior. These results combine to imply that information experiments with passive control groups can be greatly misleading about preferences and can even have the wrong sign: in my experiment, reducing overoptimism about an attribute nonetheless boosts demand for its associated good. I show, both theoretically and experimentally, that active control-group experiments yield preference estimates with the correct sign but biased magnitudes. Finally I show that parallel active control-group experiments (PACEs) can solve this problem: PACEs yield unbiased estimates of preferences under an equal induced-attention assumption, which is testable (and satisfied) in my experiment.

articles.title: Propagation of Immigration Shocks through Firm-to-Firm Trade Networks,
articles.authors: Yusuf Emre Akgündüz, Abdurrahman B Aydemir, Seyit Mümin Cilasun, Murat Güray Kirdar
articles.abstract: This paper investigates the extent to which an immigration shock to a region propagates through supply chains. Using the unexpected arrival of Syrian refugees, who are densely concentrated in border regions of Turkey, we estimate how firms across the country are affected in terms of sales, employment, and wages. We also examine the impact of the shock on interprovincial trade, focusing on trade volume and network formation. The results reveal positive spillover effects of immigration for firms with pre-existing links to Syrian refugee-hosting regions through upstream and downstream supply chain connections. Furthermore, we find evidence that the shock expands inter-provincial trade and contributes to the formation of new firm-to-firm linkages between provinces. Finally, we show that traditional spatial approaches that compare regions with differing migration rates may conflate cross-province propagation with the direct effect of migrants; in our setting, this conflation overstates direct effects on sales and employment at both the firm and regional levels of aggregation and masks a negative direct wage effect at the firm level.

articles.title: Independent Ageing Amongst Older Adults Who Live Alone: Social Networks and Support in Singapore
articles.authors: Samantha Shu Fang Lim, Grace En Ying Chan, Siyao Gao, Vincent Chua, Chen‐Chieh Feng, Elaine Lynn‐Ee Ho
articles.abstract: This paper examines how older adults who live alone draw on local and extra‐local social ties—including kinship relations, community networks, and friendships—to age independently in Singapore. Conceptually, it engages with extant debates on the hierarchical‐compensatory and task‐specific theories. The paper draws on a mixed‐methods study that combines survey data with qualitative data from interviews, observations and GPS tracking of participants who live in two neighbourhoods. We show how older adults who live alone access and mobilise support in response to their changing life circumstances. Our findings indicate that older adults who live alone are not passive. Rather, they maintain their independence through interdependent relationships with a range of local and extra‐local social networks, which are fluid and will evolve over time. Emotional closeness determines most of all how positively older adults perceive and experience care and support. This paper demonstrates the importance of considering emotional proximity, changing social networks, and interdependence in understanding how older adults age independently.

articles.title: Friend and Neighbour Ties Among Unpartnered, Childless and ‘Kinless’ Older Adults in Europe
articles.abstract: Declining fertility, increased geographic mobility and changes in nuclear families have contributed to the rise of older adults who are unpartnered, childless or both unpartnered and childless (‘kinless’). For this growing global population, non‐family ties such as friends and neighbours may be particularly important. Although often conflated, friends and neighbours represent distinct ties that often provide different resources, with neighbours being geographically proximal and friends being geographically flexible. Yet, very few cross‐national studies distinguish between friends and neighbours, and no study to date has examined these ties among older adults with limited family availability cross‐nationally. To address this gap, I analyze social network data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (Wave 6; N = 56,093 respondents across 17 countries) and country‐level indicators from multiple sources. Using multivariable logistic regression models, I examine whether older adults lacking partners and/or children are more likely to list a friend compared to a neighbour in their discussion networks and explore how these patterns vary across macro‐level contexts. Lacking family is associated with greater reliance on non‐family ties, and friend ties are substantially more common than neighbour ties in all countries and contexts. Friend ties are particularly more common for kinless older adults in Northern and Western Europe, especially in higher‐GDP contexts. Although neighbour ties are much less common overall, they are more pronounced in lower‐GDP and Southern European contexts. These findings highlight heterogeneity in later‐life support systems and underscore the importance of both geographically‐bounded and geographically‐flexible support ties to promote ‘aging in place’ and ‘aging in networks’, respectively.

articles.title: Geographical Mobility and Occupational Achievement: Examining the Role of Italian Cities as «Escalator» Regions
articles.authors: Rocco Molinari, Roberto Impicciatore, Nazareno Panichella
articles.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between geographical mobility and occupational achievement focusing on internal migration processes that occurred in the second half of the 20th century in Italy. Using retrospective information from the Italian Household Longitudinal Survey (IHLS), the study clarifies whether certain destinations, particularly large urban centres in central and northern Italy, provide inter‐regional migrants with systematic occupational advantages, enabling migrants to attain higher‐status positions after relocating. Findings reveal that migrants to large cities in central and northern Italy achieve, on average, higher occupational standings compared to stayers in the area of origin, with strong differences by gender and geographical area of origin. Furthermore, the occupational advantage associated with migration to large cities substantially varies by social class of origin, suggesting the interrelation between urban escalators and the intergenerational transmission of social inequalities.

articles.title: The primary premium: Why legislators are incentivized to side with primary voters over general election voters
articles.authors: Sarah E. Anderson, Daniel M. Butler, Laurel Harbridge-Yong
articles.abstract: How are legislators incentivized to behave when their primary and general electorates disagree about an issue? We argue that primary electorates are generally more unified in their issue preferences and more sensitive to roll-call positions than general electorates, incentivizing legislators to prioritize primary voters when facing conflicting demands from the two groups. Using the 2016 Cooperative Election Study and an original survey experiment with over 13,000 respondents, we show that primary voters are both more unified and more likely to adjust their vote choice based on policy alignment. When we combine electorate unity and voter sensitivity, we find that US senators had more to gain by siding with their primary electorate in 84% of the votes where they were cross-pressured. This helps explain why politicians are incentivized to cater to their primary electorate − shaping patterns of representation and policy outcomes in American politics.

articles.title: Diffusion of environmental treaty dynamism: EU and US influences
articles.abstract: Multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) can be dynamic in that they evolve with the introduction and adaptation of new legal commitments. This research contributes to explaining such treaty dynamism by exploring its diffusion across institutions. I focus on the role of the European Union (EU) and the United States (US) in the broader network of MEAs, eventually contending that dynamism diffuses more strongly through EU inter-agreement ties. The US inter-treaty network, however, is likely to play a limited role in facilitating the diffusion of new commitments. It is argued that these patterns are plausibly driven by the EU’s consistently pro-environmental agenda and its economic interests geared toward regulatory norm harmonization across MEAs. The empirical evidence is based on spatial models analyzing the most comprehensive data set of MEAs concluded since 1945. The results show that EU linkages promote treaty dynamism, whereas US ties have no significant effect on dynamism diffusion.

articles.title: Does bilateral aid work better through multilateral channels? Evidence from the GODAD database
articles.abstract: How does the choice of aid modality influence development effectiveness? While scholars have extensively studied the drivers of aid delegation, the relative effectiveness of different modalities remains under-theorized. I develop a theory of aid effectiveness rooted in the interplay of donor motives, recipient incentives, and principal−agent dynamics. I argue that earmarked aid to international organizations (IOs) will succeed in achieving specific sectoral outcomes by leveraging IO capacity to constrain recipient slack, though its rigid mandates and high transaction costs will limit its broader development impact. Conversely, bilateral aid—which often serves donor particularistic interests and grants recipients more autonomy—is generally ineffective, except when political competition disciplines recipients to prioritize long-term gains. To test these propositions, I utilize the GODAD database to analyze geolocated aid projects from 19 Western donors across 1,753 subnational regions from 1990 to 2024. Using two-step counterfactual difference-in-differences estimators, I examine the impact of different funding types on household wealth, child mortality, and governance. The findings reveal that earmarked aid is effective for specific goals, such as health aid reducing child mortality, whereas the success of governance aid depends on low baseline development levels. In contrast, bilateral aid is frequently ineffective or counterproductive, correlating with increased mortality and decreased state capacity. Sectoral targeting has limited effects, positively affecting only household wealth creation. These results highlight how the institutional design of aid delivery mediates the tension between donor control and recipient agency, offering critical implications for the study of multilateral delegation and aid effectiveness.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence, Regulatory Capacity, and the Adaptive State
articles.authors: Chris Doyle, Martin Cave, William Webb
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing not only what regulators govern but the informational environment through which regulation is conducted. Regulators increasingly use advanced analytics to process evidence and target supervisory attention, while regulated organizations deploy AI across their operations. This paper develops the concept of the adaptive regulatory state to analyze how changing informational capabilities generate behavioral and institutional adaptation. Comparative cases from financial supervision, competition, tax administration, and electronic communications identify three possible trajectories: constructive learning, governed co‐evolution, and adversarial escalation. Effective oversight does not require technological parity with regulated firms, but sufficient informational, organizational, and verification capabilities to respond as the regulatory environment changes. Four institutional principles follow: functional rather than technological capacity; effective inspectability and proportionate assurance; learning with bounded revisability; and coordinated but accountable capacity. The adaptive regulatory state is defined by whether regulatory institutions remain capable, accountable, and legitimate as their informational environment evolves.

articles.title: Contested Coexistence: Transnational Private Governance and Public Regulatory Reform in Global Value Chains
articles.abstract: This article examines how a transnational coalition of NGOs, unions, and labor rights organizations drove both private and public regulation on gender‐based violence and harassment in Lesotho's garment sector, and how the resulting regulatory systems coexist despite ongoing tension between them. Drawing on 15 months of ethnographic fieldwork, stakeholder interviews, and archival analysis, we show that the coalition leveraged reputational and diplomatic pressures, enabled by Lesotho's structural dependence on the United States as both buyer and donor, to secure the Lesotho Agreement and subsequent public regulatory reforms. The same dependencies that enabled these reforms also generated sustained tensions once the regulatory systems were in place. We term this dynamic contested coexistence —a governance configuration in which a supplying country's structural dependence on a buyer country forecloses rejection of a private regulatory system while constraining open endorsement of it—and identify it as a new form of private‐public interaction within Cashore et al.'s framework.

articles.title: Not my democracy: conceptions, discontent, and participation in Europe
articles.authors: Bernd Schlipphak, Caner Simsek, Oliver Treib
articles.abstract: Citizens differ not only in how strongly they support democracy, but also in what they expect democracy to be. Yet we know less about whether these democratic expectations shape satisfaction with democracy (SwD) and, through it, political participation (PP) in established European democracies. We first develop a mechanism linking citizens’ prioritized understandings of democracy (UoD) to SwD and unconventional political participation (UPP). Satisfaction with democracy is treated as an indicator of perceived congruence between citizens’ democratic ideals and how democracy works in practice. Second, we test this mechanism systematically in Europe using ESS Round 10 data, including almost 60,000 respondents in 31 countries. We find that (a) citizens’ conceptions of democracy affect SwD and (b) that SwD is a mediator for the impact UoD have on UPP.

articles.title: A risky business: navigating autocratization through ideological legitimation claims
articles.abstract: Autocratization typically results from measures aiming at seizing, strengthening, and consolidating political power. However, it is not without risks: it may produce adverse reactions from multiple actors and possibly lead to the fall of its perpetrators from power. What makes autocratizing incumbents more capable of surviving during such a perilous process? We argue that the adoption of ideological legitimation strategies makes incumbents more capable of surviving during autocratization in democratic and electoral authoritarian regimes. We test our argument through survival analysis of incumbents in power during processes of autocratization from 1900 to 2024. Though relatively understudied in the context of autocratization, our study highlights ideology as a key factor in the process of transformation of a political regime toward autocracy.

articles.title: Public support for novel carbon removal hinges on procedural and distributive fairness
articles.authors: Livia Fritz, Lucilla Losi, Christine Merk, Michela Boldrini, Valentina Bosetti, Chad M. Baum, Benjamin K. Sovacool
articles.abstract: Alongside the need for rapid emissions reductions, removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is emerging as a central pillar of global climate policy. Scaling up carbon removal raises pressing questions about how this can be done in an equitable and socially legitimate manner. Using vignette experiments with nationally representative surveys in six global south and global north countries ( N = 10,852 respondents across Brazil, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, Italy, Norway and the UK), we examine which modes of implementing novel carbon removal methods gain public support across diverse socio-political settings. We find that support hinges on procedural and distributive fairness: opening planning processes to public and expert scrutiny, benefit sharing and not-for-profit arrangements consistently increase public support for carbon removal across all countries and technologies. Respondents are unwilling to trade such fairness considerations for technical performance. Just governance and implementation are critical for securing public support when scaling up novel carbon removal methods.

articles.title: When Movement Widens the Gap: The Contingent Effect of the Chinese #MeToo Movement on Feminist Attitudes
articles.authors: Shuning Lu, Haixin Mu, Tian Yang
articles.abstract: Social movements are often associated with various cultural outcomes, including shifts in public opinion regarding movement-related attitudes and ideologies. This study examines the shift of feminist attitudes among the public following the Chinese #MeToo movement. We develop a sociotechnical contingency framework that emphasizes how identity-based movement relevance and access to information channels shape the shifts in public opinion following social movements. Using nationally representative data from the Chinese General Social Survey (2010–2023), we find that the #MeToo movement was significantly associated with an increase in pro-feminist attitudes. These changes were unevenly distributed across groups, revealing widening attitudinal gaps along gender identities and digital divides. Our findings contribute to a nuanced understanding of how contemporary digitally mediated movements catalyze cultural change and underscore the need to contextualize their impact as it interacts with structural dynamics.

articles.title: The End of the Observable Infodemic: Privatised Observability and Public Health Monitoring
articles.abstract: Infodemiology and infodemic management rest on a premise so foundational that it is rarely stated: health information behaviour leaves traces that researchers and public institutions can observe. This paper argues that the premise is dissolving. Health information seeking is migrating from publicly observable websites and platforms into conversational artificial intelligence, where exchanges unfold in private dyads between user and system and are visible in full only to the providers operating them. The paper develops a typology of three observability regimes, termed open, brokered and enclosed observability, which differ in trace custody, conditions of third‐party observation, attainable granularity, stability of access and the epistemic position of public health. It traces the arc from the open web through the platform era, whose brokered observability collapsed in the post‐API age, to the enclosed regime of conversational agents, in which knowledge about population health information behaviour is produced and selectively disclosed by commercial providers. The analysis derives implications for infodemic management, for the evaluation of health information environments and for regulation, and argues that privacy‐preserving research access to conversational health data should be established as public health infrastructure.

articles.title: Payoff selectivity drives collective intelligence during dynamic resource tracking in humans
articles.authors: Valerii Chirkov, Ralf H.J.M. Kurvers, Pawel Romanczuk, Dominik Deffner
articles.abstract: Humans’ abilities for complex social learning and collective adaptation stand out across species. Yet it is largely unknown how people integrate dynamically changing personal and social cues in realistic environments, resulting in collective intelligence or maladaptive behavior. Here, we report an online 3D immersive-reality experiment in which participants ( n = 621) search for and track a mobile resource under realistic visual–spatial constraints. Participants complete the task either alone or in groups of five with different types of social information and resource speeds. Contrasting earlier work, participants in groups outperform solitary individuals, but only when payoff information was available. High-resolution visual field data and movement trajectories reveal that payoff visibility prompts adaptive recalibration of visual information flow, thereby enabling flexible adaptation. Computational models of fine-grained movement decisions and agent-based simulations show that payoff information lets participants dynamically identify and selectively respond to reliable social cues, thus unlocking the group’s collective potential.

articles.title: Religiosity and local debt repayment: evidence from Italian mayors
articles.abstract: Does a politician’s religion influence their policymaking? While existing research has examined how gender, class, and ethnicity shape political decisions, the role of religiosity remains understudied. This paper investigates how religious values influence debt repayment decisions among local politicians. I develop a novel measure of individual religiosity, based on names matching local patron saints, and apply it to 62,908 candidates in Italian municipal elections. Using a regression discontinuity design, I find that narrowly elected religious Catholic mayors are more likely to increase debt repayment. This effect likely reflects two mechanisms: Catholic moral teachings, which stress the obligation to repay debt, and risk aversion rooted in religion. Overall, these findings demonstrate that religion meaningfully shapes the fiscal behavior of elected officials.

articles.title: Mapping EU biological medicines’ regulatory guidance through contributors and documents (1990/2026)
articles.authors: Valentin Brunel, Valentin Roby, Michael Morrison, Aurélie Mahalatchimy
articles.abstract: European Union Legislation in the sector of biological medicines is complemented by a substantial volume of guidance documents which are essential for strategic choices regarding biologicals development from lab to patients, especially authorisation processes as regards to quality, safety, and efficacy aspects. This corpus of guidance documents has historically been underutilised for research. Hence, the I-BioLex project has focused on both documents and actors, in a genealogical perspective. The two datasets presented in this paper gather all guidance documents relevant to this field, with comprehensive metadata, as well as a list of all contributors to public consultations conducted during the process of adoption or revision of these guidance documents in the field of biologicals at the EU level from 1990 to 2026. It constitutes an original foray into interdisciplinary research at the crossroads of social sciences (law, sociology,…) and biomedical sciences (medicine, pharmacy,…) in order to better understand how guidance documents are shaped and who is influencing them, in the field of biologicals.

articles.title: The ParlLawSpeech Parliamentary Text Data Collection > 3 Million Parliamentary Bills, Laws, and Speeches from 8 Legislatures
articles.authors: Jan Schwalbach, Lukas Hetzer, Sven-Oliver Proksch, Christian Rauh, Miklós Sebők
articles.abstract: Parliamentary texts are central sources for studying democratic representation, policy-making, and institutional decision-making, and they also constitute a highly valuable domain for natural language processing research. Despite their importance, access to comprehensive, clean, and machine-readable parliamentary corpora remains limited. This paper introduces the ParlLawSpeech (PLS) collection, a large-scale, curated corpus comprising more than three million documents from eight European parliaments, each covering over two decades. PLS extends existing parliamentary text resources in two key ways. First, it integrates full texts and metadata not only for parliamentary speeches but also for legislative bills and finally adopted laws. Second, it provides systematic data linkage across these document types, enabling researchers to trace the full parliamentary decision-making process from draft legislation through debate to adoption. Covering seven national parliaments and the European Parliament, PLS offers a uniquely rich resource for political science and advanced NLP research.

articles.title: Lobbying by Rebel Groups in the United States: Introducing the Rebel Lobbying Dataset, Version 1, 1945–2012
articles.authors: Yu Bin Kim, Ilayda B. Onder
articles.abstract: During civil wars, some rebel groups hire lobbying and public relations (PR) firms to cultivate favorable perceptions abroad. Almost 15% of rebel groups, for example, lobbied through PR firms at least once in the United States between 1945 and 2012. Yet, data limitations have made it difficult for scholars of rebel diplomacy to study rebel lobbying systematically. To help mitigate these limitations and facilitate future research, we introduce the first version of the Rebel Lobbying Dataset (RLD), which captures whether and when rebel groups hired professional lobbying firms in the United States. The RLD covers 230 rebel groups engaged in 103 civil conflicts worldwide from 1945 to 2012. After presenting several descriptive patterns, we demonstrate the dataset’s utility by examining whether rebel lobbying in Washington is associated with subsequent U.S. support for rebel groups. By making rebel groups’ use of professional lobbying firms visible at scale for the first time, the RLD opens new avenues for studying the determinants, timing, and consequences of how rebel groups pursue foreign influence.

articles.title: Social Physiology: Human homeostasis is more efficient in social proximity
articles.authors: Monia Masalha, Matan Cohen, Maayan Aloni, Einav Toledo, Ella Stahl, Diane Shachar, Or Eliav, Shai Fuchs, Shir Atzil
articles.abstract: Physiological homeostasis is traditionally viewed as an individual process optimized through evolution to minimize the energetic costs of regulation. However, it remains unknown whether social proximity enhances the efficiency of homeostatic regulation, including in systems not traditionally viewed as socially sensitive. Glucose metabolism is one such system. In a set of preregistered experiments, we found that glucose homeostasis following a carbohydrate challenge is more efficient in a Social condition than an Alone condition, exhibiting lower perturbation amplitude and faster recovery ( n = 108). The social benefit in homeostasis replicated in thermoregulation during a cold challenge ( n = 116) and in sympathetic regulation during stress in adults ( n = 115) and infants ( n = 56). These findings demonstrate Social Physiology, a cross-domain principle whereby physiological homeostasis is more efficient in social proximity. Evolutionarily, Social Physiology reveals a psychobiological benefit of sociality, beyond its behavioral and ecological advantages, that may contribute to the emergence and maintenance of social bonds.

articles.title: Far-right political support and clean technology adoption in Germany
articles.authors: Sebastian Reining, Moritz Wussow, Chad Zanocco, Benedikt Kau, Rita Sousa-Silva, Corinna Köpke, Sahani Pathiraja, Dirk Neumann
articles.abstract: The diffusion of clean technologies is critical for climate goals, yet political polarization influences adoption. Here we examine how ideology affects residential solar photovoltaic (PV) and electric vehicle (EV) uptake in Germany, drawing on responses from a three-wave individual-level survey, municipality-level observations of PV and EV registrations and election results. Supporters of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) show significantly lower willingness to adopt EVs and, to a lesser degree, PV systems compared with supporters of the pro-environmental Bündnis 90 / Die Grünen (GRÜNE) party. However, polarization is not static. The relative adoption gap between municipalities with strong AfD support and those with strong GRÜNE support declined from 76% to 31% for solar PV between 2000 and 2023, and from 84% to 60% for EVs between 2015 and 2019. Here, using an instrumental-variable strategy based on wolf attacks as a predictor of AfD vote share, we provide complementary evidence on the relationship between far-right voting and the adoption of clean technology. Counterfactual simulations indicate that, by 2023, solar PV diffusion could have been up to 1.3% higher and EV diffusion up to 2.9% higher in the absence of rising electoral support for the far right.
